Press Release:


It’s a tradition passed on from generation to generation: a fearless band of travelling minstrels in northern Nigeria who have the seemingly magical ability to handle hyenas. Carte Blanche finds out more about the little known and seldom filmed Hyena Handlers.

Script:


Hyena Boys
Transcripts

00:00:10:18 – 00:00:21:13
Voice over 1
This is a story unique to Nigeria; A story of men, women and children being brought together to practice the ancient art of taming the beasts.

00:00:21:20 – 00:00:35:12
Mohammed: They call us the ones with baboons, hyenas and snakes.
I saw my father working...
I saw what he was doing and I learnt everything from him.

00:00:36:00 – 00:01:04:00
Voice over 2
It’s in the north of Nigeria, near Abuja, where we track down one family of hyena handlers.
Mohammed is the leader of this tribe. Having taken these men, women and children under his wing, he dedicates his time to teaching them the art of taming the wild beasts. Together, they form a tight-knit family and, although he isn’t biologically related to each member, Mohammed plays father to all who live in the camp.

00:01:06:00
Mohammed: My children also do this work.
Everything I know how to do, they can also do.

00:01:17:23 – 00:01:36:02
Mufasa: I have been doing this since I was 5.
The hyena was also little when he started to practice with me.
His name is James.
Since he was little, I've been feeding him.
And he got used to me.

00:01:41:15
Hyena Growls
Mufasa: I will deal with you






00:01:49:22 – 00:02:39:17
ABDULLAHI BARAU: I am the head of the snake handlers.
I teach this boy.
I teach every one of them because I am the teacher.
I started when I was 10 years old.
Now I'm 32 years old.
My dad gave me medicine that I drank.
That's when I went to the bush.
Any snakes that I see, I'll catch them without fail.
Baboons, hyenas... Everything.
I'll just catch them without fail.


00:02:47:09 – 00:03:07:10
Aisha (Mohammed’s wife): My name is Aisha, I am Baba Mohammed's wife.
He met me through my dad. My
dad also does the same job as him.
It's been 8 years since I started playing with the animals.
I started with snakes.
Then I moved from snakes to scorpions.

00:03:07:14 – 00:03:22:03
Voice Over 3
Aisha’s father taught her how to tame the beasts when she was a child, before she was given to Mohammed, to be his wife, at fourteen years old. Now, she will pass on the knowledge of the ancient techniques to her own children.

00:03:22:18 - 00:03:45:17
Aisha (Mohammed’s wife): He took the medicine from when he was little.
After his bath we will rub the medicine on him.
The medicine will guide him when he grows up.
When he starts playing with the snakes,
the monkeys, the hyenas...
the baboons and the rest of them.
The name of the medicine is bauri.





00:03:48:21 – 00:58:22
Aisha (Mohammed’s wife): For now his senses are not up to it.
But when the snake is in front of him
he can touch it and play with it.
It will do him no harm.

00:04:01:04 – 00:04:11:22
Mohamed: We use medicine to help us.
We drink the medicine before we go.
Then we can enter and catch them.
We give the animals medicine to drink.
And we drink it too.

00:04:12:24 – 00:04:27:04
Voice Over 4
Mohammed and his family, like the other troupes of Hyena Handlers in the North of Nigeria, then use the animals to perform in a kind of traveling circus. They move around Nigeria entertaining the masses.

00:04:27:21 –
Mufasa: We perform together everywhere.

00:04:35:14 – 00:04:47:20
Mufasa: We are tying them up because some people are scared.
In case it catches someone.
That's why we are tying them up.
Because this one is wicked.

00:05:04:13 – 00:05:17:01
Mufasa: We are turning the animal and playing with it.
When it plays, it will turn around and hug us.

00:05:21:01 – 00:05:32:17
Mufasa: We also sell the snakes, hyenas and baboons.
We go to the bush, we catch them. We sell them to the
rich ones who keep them in a cage for their kids.
Their kids see them and they get happy.





00:05:32:17 – 00:05:41:00
Voice Over 5
This is a family run business; the scarier the animals, the bigger the tricks, and the more money Mohammed and his family can earn.

00:05:42:17 – 00:05:56:19
Mohammed: Some come to take us away to perform for them.
What we gain from it depends...
We can get $8000, $5000, $3000 from them.
We use the money to survive.

00:05:57:10 – 00:06:21:12
Voice Over 6
Of course, the relationship between man and animal is complex. The men in this tribe speak of experiencing a spiritual connection with the animals they train. But, in order to overpower the animals, to ensure they are obedient to them, the men must break them down, often brutally. It’s similar to the way in which circus animals are trained to listen to their ringleader.

00:06:21:21 – 00:06:26:24
Mufasa: I will beat him if he misbehaves,
but if he does nothing I don't beat him.

00:06:31:19 – 00:06:52:01
Mohammed: They like us. When we're not around they miss us.
And we like them too. We also miss them.
Like when the others take them to perform.
We hope they come home safely.
Even those who took them out as well.
That is our prayer.
Even if it's just one.
We pray for it to come back safely.

00:06:53:24 – 00:07:19:13
Voice Over 7
Because the hyena handlers are nomadic, very few people have been able to document their way of life. It is rare to get such an intimate glimpse into their world.
But, no matter what we feel about the practice, the animals or even how they are treated, the reality is that this is a crucial means of survival for Mohammed and his family. And they will continue the practice for generations to come.

00:07:20:06 – 00:07:33:00
Mohammed: This trade doesn't just start now.
It starts when we are little.
Our parents teach us so that we can eat.
Now we are teaching the younger ones.
Everyone can learn. This is our work.

00:07:35:13 – 00:07:39:05
Mohammed: This is our work and we will continue doing it.
